task: Matrix sparsification: given the operator U of a fast multiplication algorithm, find an invertible V minimising nnz(U V)
source: Produced by `reproduce/measure.py`, which runs `sparsify-operator fixtures/<name>.matrix` once per operator.
why: Fewer nonzeros in the operator means fewer additions in the algorithm it encodes, which is the cost the multiplication count does not capture.
machine: Single core of a 12th Gen Intel i5-12450H at 2.2 GHz.
methods: Exact, matroid greedy over Q: scan column supports in ascending size and keep every codeword that raises the rank. The minimum over every invertible V, by Rado-Edmonds, and the only method here proved so.

The three methods removed on 2026-08-22 (row-basis heuristic, and both of [beniamini2020]'s oracles) reached the same counts 88x to 343x more slowly and are archived on the rejected-experiments branch under retired/dominated_sparsifiers/, with their measurements; see matrix_sparsification/dominated.md.

published_scheme_operators.scheme: 3x3x3_23_Grey-221, a published rank-23 <3,3,3> scheme, as its three encoding operators
published_scheme_operators.source: Carried, and every column of it. The three operators are PLinOpt's own and are not among the twelve fixtures/plinopt/ ships, so no run here re-derives as_given or minimum either; PLinOpt's own bin/sparsifier is not built in the checkout vendored here, so the plinopt column needs that tool built first. All three columns were measured on this machine on 2026-08-22 under MEASURING.md, and reproduce/questions.py names this block in CARRIED so a run says on every pass that it left it alone. What each column means and how P had to be oriented: matrix_sparsification/measured-with-other-tools/the-nonzero-counts.md.
published_scheme_operators.why_here: index.html typesets the as_given and minimum columns by hand, so a reader with no JavaScript sees the evidence, and until this block existed they sat in no results file and nothing checked them. reproduce/front_page.py now holds the page's table and the sentence above it to this block, and adds the column totals rather than reading a fourth row, so a total that stops adding up fails. The plinopt column is recorded here and asserted against no page.

readings: The strand has a number now. Strassen's two encoding operators go from 12 nonzeros to 10; the alternative-basis operator goes from 21 to 10. Every route reaches the same 10, and every result is checked to have the same row space as the operator it came from.

Ten is what the row-basis construction predicts rather than a surprise: inverting a square block of rows makes four rows singletons, and the remaining three come out with two nonzeros each. Ten is what the construction predicts rather than a surprise, and the matroid greedy proves it minimal.
The runs take milliseconds because field operations on small matrices (7×4) are cheap compared to the minimisation over a discrete space.

The operators no longer have to be typed in. The rank search recovers L and R from the decomposition it finds and writes them out, so deriving a fast algorithm and then reducing its additions is two commands. On F2 5x5 that is 25 multiplications down to 14, and the left operator's 31 nonzeros down to 27.
corrections: Algorithm 2.4 was unreachable. Both branches of the prompt that offers the choice call algorithm 2.3, so the top-down oracle could never run from the command line.
Its search returns None when it finds no candidate, into a caller that unpacks the result into two variables. It does not fire on these operators, so it was latent rather than observed.

The search objective counts zeros exactly by testing field equality, not floating-point equality. Using `== 0` on raw doubles can miscount: on the alternative-basis operator this sees 86 zeros where 144 exist, even with post-rounding applied. The reported count can be sound while the objective being maximised is not.
limits: The matroid greedy over Q returns the minimum over every invertible V and stops on collecting a basis rather than on a proof that nothing lighter exists, so it does not finish on an operator whose greedy weights are large: 4x4x4_49_156_L needs weight 6 or more for 7 of its 16 vectors, and the command now refuses that operator in milliseconds rather than running on. --simplex answers it instead, by linear programming, in 0.34 s and at 100 nonzeros. That is an UPPER BOUND: it would be the minimum if the operator's column matroid were regular, and it is not, a sixteen-column minor having determinant -2. What is verified rather than assumed is that the answer spans the same row space. The greedy by rescaling, behind --operations, guarantees nothing and minimises nnz + nns rather than nnz, which is why speed does not order it against the rest. See matrix_sparsification/method/answering-without-searching.md.

provenance.protocol: one core, fastest of three, quiet machine. See MEASURING.md.

counts_provenance.covers: The counts in this file and the invocations that produced them, and nothing else. Every `seconds` field here is older than this block and was not touched: a count is exact arithmetic and comes out the same on any machine, a timing does not, so `--counts` refreshes the first and leaves the second exactly as measured. What produced the timings is the `provenance` block.
counts_provenance.protocol: counts only: exact arithmetic, one run each, the machine irrelevant.
